title: Because, when, if
goal: Join two sentences into one with conjunctions of time, cause, condition, and contrast, and use the linking words that may not stand first.
bekal: put *enim*, *igitur*, and *autem* in the right place
build long sentences that stay clear

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Cur non venisti?
dialogs.intro: Sextus didn't show up yesterday, and everyone has a theory about why.

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.id: Why didn't you come yesterday, Sextus?

lines.speaker: Sextus:
lines.id: Because I was sick. My head hurt.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Ubi aeger es, domi manere debes.
lines.id: When you're sick, you should stay home.
lines.literal: when sick-masc are-you, at-home stay must-you.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Sextus semper aeger est ubi labor adest!
lines.id: Sextus is always sick when there's work to do!
lines.literal: Sextus always sick-masc is-he when work be-here-it!

lines.speaker: Sextus:
lines.text: Non verum est! Cum labor adest, ego adsum.
lines.id: That's not true! When there's work, I'm there.
lines.literal: not true-neut is-it! when work be-here-it, I be-here-I.

lines.speaker: Sextus:
lines.text: Dormio quia nocte lego. Libri enim boni sunt.
lines.id: I sleep because I read at night. The books are good, you see.
lines.literal: sleep-I because night-in read-I. book-pl for good-pl are-they.

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Si libros legis, bene est. Quamquam nocte dormire melius est.
lines.id: If you read books, that's good. Although sleeping at night is better.
lines.literal: if book-pl-obj read-you, good is-it. although night-in sleep better-neut is-it.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: After we've had dinner, we'll read a story.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Sextus manet ubi cena est. Semper enim esurit.
lines.id: Sextus stays when there's dinner. He's always hungry, you see.
lines.literal: Sextus stay-he when dinner is-it. always for be-hungry-he.

lines.speaker: Sextus:
lines.text: Verum dicis. Amicus tamen vester sum!
lines.id: True. But I'm still your friend!
lines.literal: true-neut-obj say-you. friend however your-pl-masc am-I!

notes: **Quod and quia both mean "because".** They are interchangeable, and both are followed by an ordinary verb — no special form to learn. Watch out for one thing: *quod* also means "which" in the neuter (Unit 15) and "what". The sentence tells you which.

**Ubi and cum both mean "when".** *Ubi* also means "where", and *cum* also means "with" — two words doing double duty. If *cum* is followed by just a noun, it means "with"; if it's followed by a whole clause, it means "when".

**Enim, igitur, tamen, autem never stand first.** Look at *libri enim boni sunt* ("for the books are good") and *amicus tamen vester sum* ("but I'm still your friend"). These linking words always go after the first word of their sentence. It's a very distinctive habit, and it instantly makes your writing sound Latin.

**Dum tu dormis, nos laboramus.** *Dum* means "while" and is almost always followed by a present-tense verb, even when the story is about the past. So *dum legebam* does exist, but *dum lego* is far more common — and it still means "while I was reading".

blocks.text: Every conjunction in this unit is followed by an ordinary verb, just as you've learned. No new forms; the only new thing is how to build long sentences.

rows: Before you go out, have a drink.
As soon as he came, he shouted.

blocks.text: *Dum spiro, spero* is one of the Latin sentences most often carved on buildings and badges. Now you can take it apart yourself: *spiro* ("I breathe"), *spero* ("I hope"), *dum* ("as long as"). Three words, one promise.

head: Latin
Meaning
Example
Translation
rows: I didn't come because I was sick.
If you come, I'll be glad.
If you don't come, I'll be sad.
Although he was sick, he came.

blocks.text: The second row contains a form you haven't learned — *sis*, the subjunctive of *es*. Latin uses that special form when *cum* means "because", but not when it means "when". For now, just recognize it; it's taught fully at the next level.

blocks.title: Pairs that always come together
items: *et … et …* — "both … and …". *Et Marcus et Iulia veniunt.*
*aut … aut …* — "either … or …". *Aut nunc aut numquam.* ("Now or never.")
*non solum … sed etiam …* — "not only … but also …". *Non solum legit sed etiam scribit.*
*tam … quam …* — "as … as …". *Tam fortis quam frater est.*

blocks.text: English puts "so", "but", and "for" at the start of a sentence. Latin has two groups: those allowed first, and those never first.

head: Can start a sentence
Meaning
Almost never starts a sentence
Meaning
rows: usually second, but both may start a sentence

blocks.text: Look at *-que* in the last row. It's not a separate word but is attached to the end of the second word: *Senatus Populus**que** Romanus* — "the Senate and People of Rome", four words shortened to SPQR on every building and every Roman army standard.

This rule seems trivial, but it is one of the quickest signs that separates real Latin from made-up Latin. *Tamen* and *igitur* are looser — Cicero, Sallust, and Tacitus often start sentences with them — while *enim*, *autem*, *vero*, *quoque*, and *-que* really never stand first.
